en: A term that's less frequently encountered,
but actually pretty important when working
with large language models is the term
temperature.
You mostly encounter it if you're building
applications on top of large language
models. So if you're building an AI chatbot
yourself, for example, which you very likely
may not be doing,
but if you do that, you will see that you
can often tweak a setting called
temperature.
That controls
how
predictable the responses are that will be
sent back by the model. Because what's
important to understand is that when a large
language model produces text output, it's
actually not deterministic. The same input
text will not always yield the same output
text, as you certainly encountered many and
many times before.
The reason for that is that the large
language model does actually not produce a
single token or a sequence of tokens
as an output, but instead token candidates
where each token has a probability.
And then it chooses one of these tokens
based on those probabilities.
And with temperature, you can control how
that decision process works. That process is
also called sampling, by the way. If that
temperature value is set to a lower value,
you get more predictability because it will
essentially always choose the token with the
highest likeliness, with the highest
probability.
If you set a higher temperature, on the
other hand, then you will get more
variety in the answers that are produced by
large language models because it will more
often also choose tokens with a lower
probability.
So it simply allows you to control how
creative or predictable the model is in its
responses. Again, it's not something you can
typically tweak in tools like ChatGPT,
but it is something that happens behind the
scenes, which you can control if you are
building your own AI-powered applications.
